html:
Ouidah is a town on the coast of today's Benin, once one of the busiest ports of the Atlantic slave trade. In 1727 it was conquered by the kingdom of Dahomey, which then ran the trade through it.

Ouidah had been the port of the small kingdom of Whydah, where English, French, Dutch and Portuguese traders kept forts. King Agaja of Dahomey seized it to get direct access to European guns and goods. Dahomey's kings raided their neighbours for captives and sold them here. Estimates suggest around a million Africans were shipped out through Ouidah, many to Brazil and the Caribbean.

The Brazilian-born trader Francisco Félix de Souza became the king's agent at Ouidah in the 19th century, and families who came back from Brazil gave the town an Afro-Brazilian flavour that remains.

Today the "Route of Slaves" runs from the old market to the beach, ending at the Door of No Return memorial. Ouidah is also a centre of Vodun, with its Temple of Pythons and a yearly Vodun festival.
